material.name: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloys
material.composition: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi with 2.0 atomic % oxygen or nitrogen

intervention.description: blended with 2.0 atomic % (at %) oxygen or nitrogen, respectively

structure.description: solid-solution phases with intrinsically highly distorted lattices

evidence_units.mechanism: The intrinsically highly distorted lattices increase solubility for interstitial atoms, which substantially impede dislocation movement. Ordered interstitial complexes-mediated strain hardening contributes to improved mechanical performance. The high configurational entropy stabilizes solid-solution phases, particularly at elevated temperatures.
evidence_spans: Here, we report about a previously undiscovered class of high-damping alloys that are both mechanically strong and workable at high temperatures. The current alloy design concept has been realized in the form of a set of model Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs blended with 2.0 atomic % (at %) oxygen or nitrogen, respectively. These high-damping HEAs show a good combination of high-temperature damping capacity, i.e., their peak damping capacity is as high as ~0.030 at a peak temperature of nearly 800 K, along with excellent mechanical properties (tensile yield strength, ~1400 MPa; elongation, ~20%).

material.name: base HEA
material.initial_state: single-phase bcc structure with 0.377 at % oxygen contamination

intervention.description: Temperature-dependent damping capacity measured by multifunction internal friction apparatus

structure.description: single-phase bcc structure with trace oxygen interstitials

evidence_units.mechanism: stress-induced position switch of interstitial atoms (Snoek damping)

conditions.strain_rate: derived from frequency 1.0 Hz and strain 2 × 10 −4

evidence_spans: Specifically at 1.0 Hz, the tanδ max of the reference HEA Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi reaches a high damping value of 0.014.
Figure 1 (A to C) illustrates the temperature-dependent variation of damping capacity tanδ of the three HEAs.
The data also reveal that the relaxation peaks are thermally activated since the peak temperature increases while the peak height (i.e., tanδ max ) decreases with increasing vibration frequency.
Such a frequency-dependent damping behavior is characteristic of strain relaxation damping, i.e., Snoek damping ( [29] ).

This suggests that the current HEAs are Snoek-type high-damping alloys in which the stress-induced position switch of interstitial atoms gives rise to the corresponding internal friction peaks ( [11] ).

The base HEA used as reference material also shows a Snoek-type damping behavior, which might be due to the trace oxygen contamination from the fabrication process, as confirmed by the data shown in table S1.

The measurements were conducted on a multifunction internal friction apparatus by the forced vibration at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, respectively. The maximum strain amplitude is 2 ×10 −4 , and the heating rate is 2 K min −1 in the measured temperature range.
According to the anelastic nature of the Snoek-type strain relaxation process ( [29] ), the activation energy H is proportional to the peak temperature T p .
For interstitial atoms in a host bcc lattice, the activation of the corresponding stress-induced reorientation process determines the peak temperature T p .

material.name: N-2 HEA
material.initial_state: single-phase bcc structure with nitrogen doping

intervention.description: Temperature-dependent damping capacity measured and microstructure analyzed via STEM

structure.description: single-phase bcc structure with ordered nitrogen complexes
microstructure: ordered nitrogen complexes (at lower frequency than oxygen clusters)

evidence_units.mechanism: stress-induced reorientation of nitrogen atoms with higher energy barriers compared to oxygen, leading to a distinct high-temperature Snoek peak and an additional low-temperature peak

conditions.strain_rate: derived from frequency 1.0 Hz and strain 2 × 10 −4

evidence_spans: The addition of oxygen or nitrogen effectively further enhances the damping capacity, and the tanδ max value at 1.0 Hz of the O-2 and N-2 HEAs increases to 0.020 and 0.027, respectively.
The white arrows in (B) and (C) indicate the additional low-temperature peak in the (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) 98 O 2 and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) 98 N 2 HEAs, respectively.
The different internal friction peaks correspond to different mechanisms behind the underlying atomic relaxation steps of the interstitials.
Thus, the occurrence of additional peaks indicates the presence of different types of stress-induced reorientation processes ( [29] ).
This effect leads to a Snoek signal in the current HEAs where the relaxation peaks are much broader than a Debye peak.

This observation shows that the high variety of local atomic configurations in these complex solid-solution alloys has a substantial effect on the variety of the resulting thermally activated site switching events.
The activation energy H is estimated to be 2.06, 2.40, and 4.06 eV for the reference alloy and the interstitially doped O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.

The activation energy H of the N-2 HEA is much higher than that of the base and O-2 HEA, implying that the nitrogen atoms switch their positions at higher barriers than oxygen in the Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA matrix.
Unexpectedly, we also observed ordered nitrogen complexes in the N-2 material (see fig. S1), although at a much smaller frequency compared to the oxygen clusters observed in the O-2 alloy.
The analysis shows that the current high-entropy damping alloys can be used at a much higher temperature (737, 747, and 730 K for the base, O-2, and N-2 HEAs at 1.0 Hz, respectively.)

material.name: O-2 HEA
material.initial_state: single-phase bcc structure with ordered oxygen complexes

intervention.description: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile test at room temperature

structure.description: single-phase bcc structure with ordered oxygen complexes

evidence_units.mechanism: solid-solution strengthening by interstitial oxygen and high strain hardening due to ordered oxygen complexes impeding dislocation motion
evidence_spans: Figure 3A shows the true tensile stress-strain curves of the current HEAs.
The base HEA, used here as reference material, shows a yield strength of ~810 MPa at an elongation of ~10.8%, which is superior to that of other Ti-Nb alloys reported to date ( [43] ).
The interstitial doped HEAs have a strong solid-solution strengthening, i.e., the yield strength was increased to 1138 and 1362 MPa for the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.
The addition of either oxygen or nitrogen to the base HEA did not appreciably deteriorate the work hardening behavior.

Particularly, the ductility of the O-2 HEA was unexpectedly doubled, which has been earlier associated with the formation of ordered interstitial complexes that provide high strain hardening ( [22] ).
Compared with the Ti-25Nb- x O at % Snoek-type high-damping alloys ( [12] ), the overall mechanical properties of the interstitially alloyed HEAs are substantially enhanced.
The interstitial doped HEAs retain the same level of ductility but display 70 to 105% higher yield strength than Ti-25Nb-1.5O alloy.

material.name: N-2 HEA
material.initial_state: single-phase bcc structure with ordered nitrogen complexes

intervention.description: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile test at room temperature

structure.description: single-phase bcc structure with ordered nitrogen complexes

evidence_units.mechanism: solid-solution strengthening by interstitial nitrogen and ductility retention due to ordered nitrogen complexes impeding dislocation motion
evidence_spans: Figure 3A shows the true tensile stress-strain curves of the current HEAs.
The base HEA, used here as reference material, shows a yield strength of ~810 MPa at an elongation of ~10.8%, which is superior to that of other Ti-Nb alloys reported to date ( [43] ).
The interstitial doped HEAs have a strong solid-solution strengthening, i.e., the yield strength was increased to 1138 and 1362 MPa for the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.
Interstitial reinforcement by nitrogen is more effective than that conveyed by oxygen doping.
The addition of either oxygen or nitrogen to the base HEA did not appreciably deteriorate the work hardening behavior.
In addition, the large ductility of the nitrogen-containing N-2 HEA is retained, which is attributed to the appearance of ordered nitrogen complexes that impede dislocation motion (see below).
Compared with the Ti-25Nb- x O at % Snoek-type high-damping alloys ( [12] ), the overall mechanical properties of the interstitially alloyed HEAs are substantially enhanced.
The interstitial doped HEAs retain the same level of ductility but display 70 to 105% higher yield strength than Ti-25Nb-1.5O alloy.

material.name: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA
material.initial_state: base HEA with low interstitial alloying content (~0.377 at %)

intervention.description: Anelastic relaxation spectra measurement at 1.0 Hz

structure.description: Two decomposed peaks resolved at 710 and 798 K
defects: impurities from synthesis process and raw materials

evidence_units.mechanism: jumps of the randomly distributed interstitial atoms in the absence of ordered interstitial complexes
evidence_spans: Figure 5 (A to C) shows the anelastic relaxation spectra (at 1.0 Hz) of the base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi, O-2 (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) 98 O 2 , and N-2 (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi) 98 N 2 HEAs as the sum of decomposed peaks.
For the base HEA, two peaks could be resolved at 710 and 798 K, respectively (see green and magenta curves in Fig. 5A ).
As there is no ordered interstitial complex in the base HEA, the two decomposed peaks probably originate from the jumps of the randomly distributed interstitial atoms.
These impurities come from the synthesis process and raw materials.
The height of the two Snoek damping peaks is 0.014 and 0.006, respectively.

intervention.description: Anelastic relaxation spectra measurement at 1.0 Hz

structure.description: Low-temperature peak at 577 K and high-temperature peaks at 748 and 850 K

evidence_units.mechanism: formation of ordered oxygen complexes gives rise to the additional low-temperature peak; randomly distributed oxygen atoms produce the two high-temperature peaks
evidence_spans: In the material with 2.0 at % oxygen, i.e., in the O-2 HEA, a low-temperature peak (red curve in Fig. 5B ) appears at 577 K, in addition to the two high-temperature peaks (green and magenta curves in Fig. 5B ) that occur at 748 and 850 K, respectively.
The formation of ordered oxygen complexes gives rise to the additional low-temperature peak ( [22] ), and the randomly distributed oxygen atoms produce the two high-temperature peaks.
The height of the additional peak and of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.005, 0.020, and 0.002, respectively.
The maximum peak height of the O-2 HEA (i.e., 0.020) is higher than that of the base HEA (i.e., 0.014).
Therefore, the higher peak height of the O-2 HEA is due to its higher oxygen content, compared to the base HEA (see table S1).

intervention.description: Estimation of oxygen atom participation in ordered complexes based on peak height ratios

structure.description: Ordered oxygen complexes formed by ~18.5% of oxygen atoms

evidence_units.mechanism: ordered interstitial complexes contribute to the enhancement of ductility

outcome.measurement_method: inferred from peak height ratio analysis

evidence_spans: as estimated by the ratio between the peak height of the additional peak and the total peak height, ~18.5% of all the oxygen atoms in the O-2 HEA participate in the formation of ordered oxygen complexes, enabling the enhanced ductility of this material ( [22] ).

intervention.description: Anelastic relaxation spectra measurement at 1.0 Hz

structure.description: Additional low-temperature peak and two high-temperature peaks observed

evidence_units.mechanism: formation of ordered nitrogen complexes and relaxation of randomly distributed nitrogen atoms
evidence_spans: For the nitrogen-doped N-2 HEA, an additional low-temperature peak (blue curve) and two high-temperature peaks (green and magenta curves) were also observed (see Fig. 5C ).
The peak height of the additional low-temperature peak is 0.002, and that of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.027 and 0.009, respectively.
Hence, only ~5.3% of all the nitrogen atoms in the N-2 HEA contribute to the formation of ordered nitrogen complexes.
As most of the nitrogen is interstitially randomly distributed, the N-2 HEA shows the strongest damping peak among all three HEAs studied here.

intervention.description: Analysis of strengthening and ductility relative to O-2 HEA

structure.description: Limited ordered nitrogen complexes and high concentration of randomly distributed nitrogen atoms

evidence_units.mechanism: larger atomic size of nitrogen leads to higher strengthening; limited ordered nitrogen complexes prevent obvious deterioration of ductility
evidence_spans: With the addition of 2.0 at % nitrogen, the larger atomic size of nitrogen (atomic radius of 0.75 Å) compared to that of oxygen (0.65 Å) leads to higher strengthening; thus, the yield strength of the N-2 HEA is ~224 MPa higher than that of the O-2 HEA.
Moreover, ~94.7% of the nitrogen atoms are randomly distributed across the interstitial sites.
As a result, the N-2 HEA exhibits both improved tensile yield strength (σ y ~ 1362 MPa) and damping properties (tanδ max ~ 0.027 at 1.0 Hz).
In addition, the ductility of the N-2 HEA (~11.9%) was not obviously deteriorated because of the formation of the limited ordered nitrogen complexes, in comparison to the base HEA.

material.name: Snoek-type high-damping HEAs
material.composition: High-entropy alloys with interstitial oxygen or nitrogen
material.initial_state: severely distorted matrices with complex chemical short-range orders

intervention.description: Comparison of peak temperature with traditional high-damping alloys

structure.description: High configuration entropy and severely distorted lattices

evidence_units.mechanism: atomic position switches of interstitials in these matrices are impeded by the high atomic-scale distortion fields, giving rise to the high activation temperatures and barrier energies for the interstitial reorientation steps
evidence_spans: It is also important to note that the peak temperature of damping in the current Snoek-type high-damping HEAs is approximately 100 K higher than that in traditional high-damping alloys ( [11] , [12] , [31] – [42] ).

Because of the high configuration entropy and severely distorted lattices of HEAs ( [50] ), atomic position switches of interstitials in these matrices are impeded by the high atomic-scale distortion fields ( [51] ).
This effect gives rise to the high activation temperatures and barrier energies for the interstitial reorientation steps and the resulting high-temperature damping capability.

material.initial_state: single-phase bcc structure with oxygen doping

intervention.description: Temperature-dependent damping capacity measured and microstructure analyzed via STEM and APT

structure.description: single-phase bcc structure with compositional clusters and ordered oxygen complexes
microstructure: compositional clusters of metallic elements (Zr, Ti rich and Ta, Nb, Hf rich)
defects: oxygen occupying interstitial sites adjacent to light atoms (Zr and/or Ti)

candidate.mechanism: stress-induced reorientation of interstitial oxygen atoms, facilitated by the presence of ordered oxygen complexes, leading to broad Snoek relaxation peaks

conditions.strain_rate: derived from frequency 1.0 Hz and strain 2 × 10 −4

Figure 4 (E to G) depicts typical results for material O-2 HEA.
Figure 4E shows a high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) micrograph with the incident electron beam aligned along the [011] bcc zone axis of the grain selected.

The Z -contrast of the STEM-HAADF image reveals the existence of light-atom–enriched regions, viz., these zones are (Zr, Ti) rich, and heavy-atom–enriched regions, i.e., (Ta, Nb, Hf) rich ( Fig. 4F ).
This means that compositional clusters of metallic elements in the O-2 HEA were formed, similar to what was reported previously ( [22] ).
The aberration-corrected STEM-ABF (annular bright field) image ( Fig. 4G ) reveals that oxygen occupies the interstitial sites in the bcc lattice (see the white arrows in Fig. 4G ).

Furthermore, statistical analysis of the STEM-HAADF and the corresponding ABF images ( Fig. 4, F and G ) confirm that oxygen tends to prefer interstitial positions adjacent to lattice sites, which are occupied by light atoms (i.e., Zr and/or Ti), accumulating to the so-called ordered oxygen complexes ( [22] ).
Figure 4 (H and I) shows the atom probe tomography analysis of the O-2 HEA.
In Fig. 4H , a set of cyan-colored isocomposition surfaces reveals regions containing more than 3.5 at % O, showing the presence of O-rich clusters, i.e., ordered oxygen complexes ( [22] ).
The appearance of an additional low-temperature damping peak in the O-2 material (see Fig. 1B ) also indicates the existence of the ordered oxygen complexes ( [22] ).
The activation energy H is estimated to be 2.06, 2.40, and 4.06 eV for the reference alloy and the interstitially doped O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.

The analysis shows that the current high-entropy damping alloys can be used at a much higher temperature (737, 747, and 730 K for the base, O-2, and N-2 HEAs at 1.0 Hz, respectively.) and wider operating temperature range (60, 53, and 30 K for the base, O-2, and N-2 HEAs at 1.0 Hz, respectively.) than any other damping material reported so far
